claims: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disease.
In multiple sclerosis (MS), the immune system attacks the protective myelin sheath covering nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord.
Multiple sclerosis (MS) causes communication issues between the brain and body.
Vision loss is a symptom of multiple sclerosis (MS).
Pain is a symptom of multiple sclerosis (MS).
Fatigue is a symptom of multiple sclerosis (MS).
Impaired coordination is a symptom of multiple sclerosis (MS).
There is no cure for multiple sclerosis (MS).
Treatments can manage symptoms of multiple sclerosis (MS).
Treatments can slow progression of multiple sclerosis (MS).
Symptoms of multiple sclerosis (MS) commonly appear between ages 20 and 40.
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is typically diagnosed between ages 20 and 40.
Blurred vision or double vision is a vision problem in multiple sclerosis (MS).
Pain with eye movement is a vision problem in multiple sclerosis (MS).
Optic neuritis is a vision problem in multiple sclerosis (MS).
Numbness is a sensory change in multiple sclerosis (MS).
Tingling is a sensory change in multiple sclerosis (MS).
Pins and needles sensations are a sensory change in multiple sclerosis (MS).
Burning sensations are a sensory change in multiple sclerosis (MS).
Sensory changes in multiple sclerosis (MS) often occur in limbs or face.
Muscle weakness is a symptom of multiple sclerosis (MS).
Difficulty with coordination is a symptom of multiple sclerosis (MS).
Difficulty with balance is a symptom of multiple sclerosis (MS).
Vertigo is an early sign of multiple sclerosis (MS).
Bladder dysfunction is an early sign of multiple sclerosis (MS).
Cognitive fatigue is an early sign of multiple sclerosis (MS).
The exact cause of multiple sclerosis (MS) is unknown.
In multiple sclerosis (MS), the immune system mistakenly attacks myelin and nerve fibers.
In multiple sclerosis (MS), attacks cause inflammation and scarring (lesions).
Multiple sclerosis (MS) can affect children.
Multiple sclerosis (MS) can affect older adults.
Women are nearly three times more likely to develop MS than men.
Having a parent or sibling with MS increases risk of MS.
MS has higher prevalence in temperate climates.
Most people with MS have a near-normal life expectancy.
Many people with MS remain active and mobile for years, particularly with modern treatments.
Most people with MS experience relapsing-remitting MS or progressive forms.
Relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) is the most common type of MS (85%).
Relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) features temporary flare-ups (relapses) followed by remission.
Secondary progressive MS (SPMS) follows RRMS.
Secondary progressive MS (SPMS) involves gradual worsening of neurological function.
Primary progressive MS (PPMS) is less common.
Primary progressive MS (PPMS) is defined by slowly worsening symptoms from the start without relapses.
Progressive-relapsing MS (PRMS) is rare.
Progressive-relapsing MS (PRMS) involves steady decline with occasional acute relapses.
